sources.news_title: Audio recordings uncover exchanges between drivers, railway control centre before Spain’s train collision
sources.text:
Published : 29 Oct 2026, 11:32 PM
Updated : 30 Oct 2026, 12:19 AM
Rescuers picked through mangled carriages on Thursday in a search for victims of Spain's second fatal high-speed train crash this year, with the death toll rising to 69 and the public demanding explanations for the latest accident.
Cranes had worked through the night to lift parts of the wreckage of Wednesday's crash, while emergency workers removed what appeared to be a body wrapped in a blanket from one of the trains in the central Spanish province of Toledo.
Regional leader Emiliano Garcia-Page said the number of deaths had risen to 69 and that human remains had been found during rescue efforts, which now involved crane operations, particularly on a carriage that remained overturned.
Among those killed in Europe's deadliest train accident since a derailment in Santiago de Compostela in 2013 was Fatima Banez, a former labour minister who chaired the social and corporate responsibility arm of Spain's employers' association.
Spain's Foreign Ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, information available so far showed, of whom one was killed and at least seven injured.
Authorities said 57 of those injured remained in hospital.
Unions Blame Lack Of Funding
The accident has added urgency to a debate about safety on Spain's railways, Europe's longest high-speed network and until recently a source of national pride.
As shocked Spaniards searched for answers on why another crash had occurred, train drivers went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety.
"We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again ... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had," said Diego Martín of the train drivers' union SEMAF.
"We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again," he said at Madrid's Atocha railway station.
Renfe, the state-run rail operator, said the strike caused significant disruption to rail services and passengers could change or cancel tickets free of charge and would be notified of affected services.
The crash, which followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line, has also upended campaigning for a November 29 snap election, with the leaders of Spain's two main parties suspending campaign events.
The Spanish government has declared three days of national mourning for those killed in the crash, which Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday happened after several trains stopped due to a signal failure. A Renfe train was then authorised to proceed at normal speed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, Puente said.
Unions blamed a lack of funding and will to improve safety, saying talks after January's crash were abandoned by the government in April.
Speaking on Wednesday, Puente rejected criticism that the Spanish railway system was unsafe, saying it was "reliable and safe...with the limits of the material itself and of human action, as is the case with any form of transport."
The government, meanwhile, has said that the decision to authorise the Renfe train to continue its journey was "inexplicable".
Pope Sends Condolences
Pope Leo sent his condolences to the families of those killed, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and conveyed his support and comfort to all affected, the Vatican said, adding he had also encouraged rescue workers to continue their efforts.
The crash prompted a major operation, which Spain's Interior Ministry said involved the deployment of more than 800 military and police personnel, over 200 vehicles, 3 helicopters, a mobile command post, drones, mounted units and search dogs.
As investigations began, a judge in Toledo barred anyone not involved in emergency, security, healthcare or judicial work from the crash site with a 2-km (1.2-mile) exclusion zone in both directions along the Madrid-Seville high-speed rail line.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who travelled to Toledo, said authorities were working "day and night" to support the victims and their families and to "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".
Meanwhile, Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, leader of the centre-right People's Party, which is currently leading in opinion polls, visited the town of Urda, where local people rushed to help with rescue efforts in the aftermath of the crash.

Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday after its second near-miss at Urda station in Toledo province this year killed 69 people and injured scores, with relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones.
One of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's rail network after the transport minister reported an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the crash.
During a visit to the crash site, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces a general election on November 29, pledged to establish the cause of the crash.
"We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again," he said.
The collision happened in the central region of Castilla-La Manchaon Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Emergency services combed through the twisted wreckage at night to find further victims on the key line linking Madrid with the southern city of Seville, hoisting pieces of mangled metal with cranes, AFP reporters saw.
Sniffer dogs and thermal drones were deployed at the crash site a few kilometres from the village of Urda on Thursday to search for bodies, the regional government said, raising the death toll to 69 from 68
Josimar Medina, a 31-year-old Peruvian who was holidaying in Spain with his girlfriend, said he was sleeping on the Renfe train when "I woke up and I was in the air."
Pablo Mejia, 42, escaped with injuries to his head, telling AFP that a last-minute change of seat saved his life.
Wearing a bloodstained grey jumper and holding his tattered suitcase, he recounted "a very strong hit... a lot of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos".
"I think I've been born again," he said.
King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia will visit train crash victims in a Toledo hospital on Thursday afternoon, the royal household said.
'Nervous and desperate'
A school in Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid, is being used to allow relatives to enquire about their loved ones.

Teams of Red Cross workers offered supportto groups of people who arrived, some of them in tears, amid crowds of police and journalists from around the world.
Red Cross psychologist Carmen Garcia said "long and hard hours" were in store because "every person will manage it in their own way.
"We have people who are in shock, who haven't taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated," Garcia said.
Jose Miguel Fernandez, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims' families.
"Many of them were calm, others were nervous and desperate. They wanted to know straight away and get news of their loved ones, he told AFP.
Safety questions
Flags flew at half-mast on public buildings, with official ceremonies and public events cancelled or scaled back.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometres (43 miles) of track, causing all trains there to be stopped.
But the control centre decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Puente said, with the Renfe train travelling 25 kilometres before striking the Iryo.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", he added.
In January, two high-speed trains collided in the southern region of Andalusia after one of them derailed and crossed onto the adjacent track, killing 46 people.
The investigation into that accident is ongoing, but the left-wing government faced heavy criticism over its management of Spain's railways.
Train drivers went on strike on Thursday "to defend rail safety". The strike had been called before Wednesday's crash.

Spain’s second deadly train crash of the year raises rail network safety concerns ahead of national election
sources.text:
Spain’s second high-speed rail disaster this year, in which one train struck another from behind, killing 69 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country’s rail network ahead of a national election.
Search teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims on Thursday, a day after the collision in central Spain. Cranes shifted the carriages as police and soldiers picked through the wreckage strewn down the gravel slope where at least three train carriages were tossed by the impact.
One more body was found overnight, taking the death toll to 69, according to the regional leader of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page. He added that 50 people remained hospitalized, while officials worked with family members to identify the dead.
“As a society, we have once again suffered a devastating blow, and we must adopt measures so that this doesn’t happen again,” Spain’s King Felipe VI said after visiting injured passengers at a hospital in Toledo.
Spain’s government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday. A minute of silence was held at various points at noon, including with lawmakers outside the Parliament and by rail workers and union leaders in Madrid’s main train station.
Testimonies of survivors filled Spanish television for a second day. Pablo López, who was on the train that was hit from behind, recounted the moment of impact and the horrific aftermath to state broadcaster TVE.
“The image I have in my head is of a person crawling on the ground after being shot out of the other train,” he said.
A second blow to Spain’s touted high-speed rail
The high-speed rail network has been considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. It is the world’s second-largest, after China’s. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
The reputation of the Spanish railways was already tarnished when in January 46 people died after one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
Then, just nine months later, came the collision Wednesday morning that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves near the village of Urda into a scene of carnage.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travellers last year, including millions of tourists.
“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Sánchez said Wednesday. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.”
Sánchez called the crash a “tragedy” when he visited the crash site a second time on Thursday, promising the victims and their families that the state would be with them.
Both deadly crashes this year took place on the same rail line between Madrid and Seville, the first of Spain’s high-speed network that opened in 1992. Each collision involved a train operated by state-owned RENFE and another operated by privately owned IRYO. Spain liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year.
Political implications for Sánchez ahead of election
Sánchez had hoped to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents when he called for early elections on Nov. 29.
He now faces questions about the safety of the railways, along with criticism from right-wing parties of his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny.
Sánchez’s main rival, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash.
Alejandro Quiroga, a professor of political science at Madrid’s Complutense University, told The Associated Press that it is too early to tell if the crash will change the minds of many voters.
“This is not good news for the Socialist Party, but it may not hurt them very much because Spaniards generally don’t like it when politicians try to take advantage of tragedies,” Quiroga said. “That could be changing, but up until now it is not seen positively.”
Government says human error caused the crash
Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente said Wednesday that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command centre for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of track stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped, with the RENFE train 25 kilometres behind.
But minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Spanish media on Thursday reproduced short audio clips of the controller ordering the train engineer to start moving.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since a “stop signal” was still active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Unions question minister
Train workers held a strike on Thursday that had already been planned before the Urda crash to demand the government carry out safety improvements to the rail services that unions say were promised after the first deadly collision in January.
Union leaders questioned the minister putting all the blame on one controller and criticized the leaking of the control room’s conversations to the media.
“The focus should not be on if there was a human error, but rather what is wrong with the system, what situations must be improved so that if there is a human error we don’t find ourselves in this situation,” said Pepa Páez of the CCOO union.
A judge also declared the crash site an investigation zone.
Meanwhile, thousands of travellers were left searching for alternative transport with the high-speed line connecting Madrid and Seville shut down.

sources.news_title: Spanish Transport Minister Blames Train Crash That Killed 68 on ‘Inexplicable’ Error
sources.text:
Spain's Transport Ministry has increased the provisional death toll from Wednesday's high-speed train collision to 69. The number of people injured is pending confirmation.
Police have appealed to family members of the crash victims to provide DNA sampling to help with the identification process. The Transport Ministry's website briefly raised the provisional death toll again to 74 late Thursday afternoon, before revising it back to 69.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said that authorities are "working day and night, not only to provide a response to the victims and their families, but to clarify every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen security so that it never happens again."
As the country's top institutions continue investigating the cause behind the collision, Transport Minister Óscar Puente has suggested that a combination of “inexplicable” human error and a computer failure was likely behind the tragedy, which occurred near Urda, Toledo, more than 80 miles south of Madrid.
Puente said in a press conference that the state-operated Renfe train slamming into the rear of a stationary private train operated by Iryo was due to an “inexplicable” order from a command center for Spain’s trains. Puente noted that the center had a computer malfunction before the order.
“It was the control center, through its operators, that made the decision to resume traffic, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” Puente said. He added later: “Clearly, it was a wrong decision.”
Puente said that they have identified the person who decided to let the Renfe train continue moving even though the Iryo one had already stopped, but he has not spoken to the control center operator. “This person is subject to whatever the investigation determines,” Puente said in the press conference.
Renfe said train services between Madrid, Ciudad Real, and Andalusia have been suspended.
The Wednesday collision is now the deadliest train crash in the country since a 2013 incident in Santiago de Compostela that killed 80 people. But the latest collision follows a similarly deadly train crash in January, which involved high-speed trains operated by the same two companies. In that crash, which occurred in Adamuz, Córdoba, 46 people died and 122 sustained injuries.
Sánchez, who visited the crash site, said his government would declare three days of mourning in response.
Despite the accident, Puente insisted that the Spanish rail system is “safe and comparable to that of other countries in our region.” However, while there are “very clear” regulations and protocols in place, he admitted, “failures can obviously occur.”
What happened?
The crashes involved a Renfe high-speed train bound for Seville with 393 people on board, and an Iryo train carrying 151 passengers. The Renfe train departed Madrid at 8:00 a.m. local time, while the Iryo train left a little earlier at 7:54 a.m., plying the same route.
Spain’s rail infrastructure uses the German LZB (Linienzugbeeinflussung) system, a railway safety technology that monitors train speeds and sends traffic instructions to the driver’s cab. Operations are meant to revert to manual control when the automated safety system fails.
Puente, in the press conference, said that at around 8:30 a.m., three computers on the railway network experienced a communication failure, taking the LZB control system offline along a 63 km (39 mi) stretch of the track. This automatically stopped about six trains traveling on that section, Puente said. The central command center would assume manual management of rail traffic.
By 8:36 a.m., the command center authorized the Renfe train to continue its journey “normally,” even though Puente says internal protocols dictate otherwise and that a “red signal” should have prevented the journey from resuming. The Renfe train had 25 km (15.5 mi) to travel before it struck the Iryo train, roughly 17 minutes later, at 8:53 a.m. The speed it reached before the impact is still unknown, but it could reach up to 200 km/h (124 mph) for that stretch of track.
What to know about Spanish high-speed rail
Spain is among the world leaders in investing in domestic high-speed rail infrastructure—defined as rails for trains that can travel 250 km/h (155 mph) and over, according to the European Commission’s Ninth Rail Market Monitoring report last year. The report shows that of European Union countries, Spain allocated the most to high-speed rail between 2018 and 2022, averaging €1.5 billion (around $1.67 billion) per year.
Latest data from the International Union of Railways shows that Spain has laid nearly 4,000 km (2,400 mi) of high-speed track, second only to China, which has laid more than 47,000 km (28,000 mi).
The European country only legally opened its domestic commercial high-speed passenger rail market to private competitors in December 2020, and Iryo became one of the commercial high-speed operators in Spain in 2022.
Spanish news outlet El Debate reported, citing data from the State Railway Safety Agency, that the number of “significant accidents” on the country’s rail network has increased over the years.

sources.news_title: Cucurella's WAG narrowly avoids being caught in deadly train crash
Cucurella’s Wife Shares Shocking Train Crash Ordeal in Spain
sources.text:
The wife of Real Madrid defender and Spanish international Marc Cucurella was traveling on a train behind the services involved in Spain’s deadly high-speed rail crash, leaving her shaken as the scale of the disaster became clear.
Claudia Rodríguez was heading from Madrid to Málaga on Wednesday morning when the collision occurred near Urda, in the province of Toledo. She later shared her experience on social media, sending support to the victims and their families as the tragedy sent shockwaves across Spain and the wider soccer world.
At least 68 people were reported dead and around 80 injured after a Renfe AVE high-speed train collided with a stationary Iryo service, according to the latest reporting from Reuters.
Rodríguez’s train was not involved in the collision, but its journey was interrupted and passengers had to return to Madrid. Her account offered a personal glimpse of a national tragedy while making clear that the experience of those who escaped harm was nothing compared with what passengers on the two affected trains endured.
What Happened on the Tracks Near Toledo
The crash occurred Wednesday morning near Urda, between Madrid and Andalucía, when a Renfe AVE train collided with an Iryo train that had stopped on the tracks. Several carriages derailed, with some falling down an embankment. Emergency crews worked through the wreckage as the number of confirmed fatalities rose, and authorities warned that the toll could change as rescue and recovery operations continued.
Spain’s government declared three days of official mourning, beginning Thursday, October 29.
The scale of the disaster has disrupted high-speed rail services between Madrid and Andalucía. Renfe activated its emergency response plan and opened assistance centers for victims’ families, while alternative transport arrangements were being prepared. The company published an official update outlining its response and providing a dedicated assistance number for affected passengers and relatives.
The official Renfe statement also confirmed that high-speed services on the affected corridor would remain interrupted.
Claudia Rodríguez’s First-Hand Account
Rodríguez, a content creator and Cucurella’s partner, was traveling to Málaga on a train following the services involved in the collision. After learning what had happened, she posted a message on Instagram expressing her shock and offering support to the victims’ loved ones.
“I was heading to Málaga on the train behind; I’m in shock. All my support to the families and friends of the victims,” she wrote, in a message reported by Spanish media. The Spanish outlet 20minutos reported her initial post and her subsequent update explaining that she was safe.
As followers asked about her condition, Rodríguez clarified that her train had not been affected because it was a considerable distance from the accident. Passengers were nevertheless forced to turn around and return to Madrid because their route was disrupted. She also reflected on how differently events might have unfolded had the collision happened later, while emphasizing that her own experience was not comparable to the suffering of those aboard the trains involved.
Cucurella and His Family Amid National Grief
The incident brought the tragedy into the orbit of a prominent soccer family, but Rodríguez’s message focused on the victims rather than her own brush with the disaster. Her decision to share information about assistance for affected passengers and relatives also helped direct attention toward those still seeking news about loved ones.
Spain has been left mourning the victims as investigators work to establish exactly how the collision occurred. The country’s royal household expressed condolences to the bereaved and support for the injured and emergency workers, while the government announced a period of official mourning. The Spanish government’s announcement formally declared three days of mourning for those killed in the crash.
All Copa del Rey matches scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday of this week have been postponed.
For Rodríguez, the immediate concern was that she and her fellow passengers were safe. For the families of those killed or injured, the consequences are immeasurably more devastating. Her account has resonated because it captures the shock of realizing how close an ordinary journey came to intersecting with an unfolding catastrophe, without losing sight of the people whose lives have been changed forever.

sources.news_title: Spain reckons with second deadly train crash ahead of national election
sources.text:
Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network.
Search teams with sniffer dogs continued to look for victims on Thursday morning, a day after the collision in central Spain. Cranes were in place to help shift the carriages as police and soldiers helped pick through the wreckage strewn down the gravel slope where at least three train carriages were tossed by the impact.
Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now.
The spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, Esther Padilla, said that 53 people remained hospitalized with 15 in critical care at different hospitals on Thursday. Padilla said the death toll remained at 68, but was still provisional.
“Emergency workers and the military emergency brigade are still working with much care because we still can’t be sure that there aren’t more victims,” Padilla told national broadcaster TVE.
Spain’s government declared three days of mourning starting Thursday.
Crash comes as Spain is preparing for an election
Spain’s high-speed rail network has been considered one of the nation’s crowning achievements. It is the world's second-largest, after China's. Until this year, it had not endured a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago.
The collision Wednesday morning that turned a sleepy stretch of rail lined by olive groves into a scene of carnage came just four weeks before the country votes in a national election.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site in the province of Toledo on Wednesday after regional authorities confirmed that more than 60 people had died and dozens more were being treated at hospitals.
In January, 46 people had died when one train jumped the track and slammed into the side of another going the opposite way in southern Spain.
Sánchez pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy like the two that have shaken trust in a rail system that carried 45 million travelers last year, including millions of tourists.
“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Sánchez said. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.”
Both deadly crashes this year took place on the same rail line. Each involved a train operated by state-owned RENFE and another operated by privately owned IRYO. Spain liberalized its high-speed rail service in 2021, with the Italian IRYO starting service the following year.
Political implications for Sánchez ahead of election
Sánchez has weathered many crises since taking power in 2018, staying in office and winning reelection after the COVID-19 pandemic and the global rise in inflation.
But polls show he faces another uphill battle when voters cast ballots in Spain's first national election since 2023. The new rail disaster can't help the prospects of his Socialist party.
Sánchez and other progressive parties had hoped to leverage a wave of discontent over housing costs and high rents when he called for early elections earlier this month.
About an hour before news of Wednesday's crash spread, Sánchez had posted on X a message that “There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country.”
He now faces questions about the safety of Spain's rail service along with criticism from right-wing parties of his liberal migration policies and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife deny.
His transport minister, Óscar Puente, faced media questions over whether he would resign following a second major train wreck under his watch. He said he was fully focused on dealing with the collision, not his future.
Sánchez's main rival, Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, demanded a full investigation of the crash on Wednesday. The conservative leader said that in respect for the victims his party canceled its campaign events for the day.
“This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families,” Núñez Feijóo said. “That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers.”
The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.
“More dead. Another tragedy. More rage over being left to fend for ourselves, the despair and the betrayal that Spaniards are enduring,” Abascal said just hours after the crash.
“I promise to work tirelessly until this government, which is a criminal organization, is sitting in a courtroom to answer for its crimes,” he said.
Human error was behind the crash
Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 39 miles stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. At that point the IRYO train was stopped near the town of Urda, while the RENFE train was 15.5 miles behind it.
But a few minutes later the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stationary IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Thousands of travelers were left stranded and searching for alternative transport after the high-speed line connecting Madrid and Seville was shut down. RENFE, which operates the most trains, is not selling tickets online for this service until mid-December.
___
Wilson reported from Barcelona, Spain. Associated Press writer Teresa Medrano in Madrid contributed to this report.

sources.text:
TOLEDO, Spain — At least 30 people are dead after a high-speed train crashed into the rear of a stopped train in Toledo in central Spain.
Two cars derailed in the crash, which was the country’s second major crash this year, The Associated Press reported. The two trains, both high-speed, were traveling in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
68 killed, dozens injured
Update 2:35 p.m. ET, Oct. 28: The death toll increased slightly to 68 people killed, with an additional 58 people treated at area hospitals for injuries, the AP reported.
The Spanish government has declared three days of national mourning.
Prime minister Pedro Sánchez said at the site, “Today all of Spain is grieving.” He also called for more safety measures concerning high-speed rail.
“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” he said.
Suspected cause
Update 11:06 a.m. ET, Oct. 28: The country’s Transport Minister said the accident was caused by an “inexplicable” order from Spain’s train central command center after a failure in a security system.
Óscar Puente said that the train engineers were not to blame, the AP reported.
Puente said the security system on 39 miles of the line stopped working because of a computer malfunction.
Despite the issue, central command told the Renfe train to run without speed restrictions. The Iryo train in front of it was not running, so the Renfe train smashed into it.
Puente said the Renfe train should not have been told to move because there was a “stop signal” on the line, or at least told to move more slowly.
Officials are trying to determine how fast the train was going at the time, the AP reported.
Death toll rises
Update 9:11 a.m. ET, Oct. 28: The death toll has risen to at least 64 people, the AP reported. The region’s central government office confirmed the latest death toll. The regional president had earlier said that 30 people had died and at least 80 people were hurt.
CNN reported that the numbers were expected to continue to rise.
Original report: One train was owned by Renfe, a state-owned company; the other was owned by Iryo, a private rail company. Both companies had been involved in a deadly crash in January. In that incident, 45 people died, making it the deadliest crash in Spain since 80 were killed in a crash in 2013.
The AP reported that the Renfe hit the Iryo train. The Iryo train was either stopped or moving at a low speed, CNN reported.
The RENFE train had 397 passengers, and the Iryo train had 147.
Spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, Esther Padilla, initially said there were 10 deaths in Wednesday’s crash but said, “that number would surely rise.”
One woman who was on one of the trains called it “awful,” saying that people were thrown in the air, CNN reported.
The woman, identified only as Patricia, said she was in the third car in the Renfe train. She said her train had been stopped for about 20 minutes before the crash because there was a lot of traffic.
“After that we departed, and maybe not after even three minutes, there was a crash,” she said, according to CNN.
“Some people were hurled into the air. Not me. I was on the left side so I suppose that’s why I wasn’t hurled in the air, but it was awful.”She added, “Some of the train structure got into our train, in our carriage, and our carriage wasn’t even the worst.”
Rail service between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia was halted due to the crash.
A shelter was opened in Urda, Toledo, with the Red Cross providing food and helping the injured, CNN reported.
People of several nationalities were on the train. Staff from the US Embassy in Spain have arrived on site.

sources.news_title: Spain: 68 Dead in High-Speed Rail Crash Points to a Systemic Problem
sources.text:
Fox News is all over this one.
Several Americans are believed to have been injured in a high-speed train collision that killed at least 68 people in Spain on Wednesday when one train collided with another that had stopped on the tracks.
The crash took place in Spain's Castilla-La Mancha, with the regional government confirming the death toll and adding that another 58 people required medical treatment in hospitals. Several Americans are believed to have been hurt in the crash, according to the State Department.
Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies, with witnesses describing a gruesome scene.
(Sigh.) Given I'm the noted railroad fan here at PJ Media, I suppose it falls to me to dig into this event. So here goes:
According to what I’ve been able to piece together, two high-speed trains collided around 8:53 a.m. local time Wednesday near Urda, in Toledo province, about 150 kilometers south of Madrid. Both were headed the same way, from Madrid to Seville. A train from Renfe, Spain’s state-owned rail company, carrying 397 people, crashed into a train from Iryo, a private operator, carrying 147 people, that had stopped on the track ahead.
At least 68 people are dead and more than 50 injured. Most of the injured were taken to a hospital in the city of Toledo, about 30 minutes away. Canada’s foreign minister said five Canadians were affected.
The early finger points at the dispatchers, not the equipment, nor the Iryo train. The line is dispatched by the government. Transport Minister Óscar Puente called the crash “truly unbelievable.” He said the preliminary investigation indicates rail controllers gave an “inexplicable” order letting one train proceed even though a safety failure had halted the other train on the tracks ahead. Officials have described it as a mix of technical and human error.
This is the second fatal disaster on the same high-speed line in less than a year, involving the same two rail operators.
In January, near Adamuz, outside Córdoba, the rear of an Iryo train derailed onto the adjacent track and was struck by an oncoming Renfe train. The minister called that crash “extremely unusual,” because it happened on a straight stretch of track recently renovated in a €700 million project, and the train was relatively new. Spain’s train drivers’ union had previously raised concerns that high speeds were causing vibration and wear and tear on high-speed lines. The death toll in that crash is reported as 45 or 46, depending on the outlet.
Today’s crash is the deadliest high-speed train crash in Spain since 2013, when a train derailed in Galicia and killed 80 people.
Of course, there’s a political aspect to this, as well. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is facing a snap election next month. He’s making the noises you’d expect him to make, saying in part that the government would investigate the cause and act “if there has been negligence,” and that Spain must restore confidence in its high-speed rail network. Expect the opposition to make the rail system’s safety record a campaign issue, especially since Renfe and the track operator ADIF are both state-run.
I also expect the investigation to take added time, given the death toll and given this is a second such incident on that line in a year and certainly the deadliest.
Need I say that Spain’s high-speed rail is the one many rail enthusiasts here in the ’States want us to copy?
In fairness, it must be said that the bad rap that mass transit options like planes and trains get in situations like this is a little unfair. A train wreck or plane crash kills dozens of people at once, in one place, on camera, and dominates the news for days. Car crashes kill roughly 40,000 Americans a year, spread out a few at a time, and almost none make the national news. Psychologists call it the availability heuristic: we judge risk by how easily examples come to mind, and the dramatic ones stick.
Then too, it must be said that a lot of this is the mainstream press amping up things, because frankly, fear sells. Alas, there are consequences of that fear as well. After 9/11, a lot of Americans got off planes and into cars. The psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer estimated that the shift caused roughly 1,600 extra highway deaths in the year that followed, more than the number of passengers killed on the four hijacked planes. He called it “dread risk.” People fear the rare catastrophe far more than the everyday danger, even when the everyday one is much more likely to kill them.
But all that said, I’m thinking we shouldn’t be quite so quick to let Spain’s government off the hook, here. 
One crash might be a fluke. The second fatal crash in a year seems somewhat less likely to be so, particularly with dispatchers apparently waving a train into an occupied block. It starts to look like a systemic problem, rather than bad luck. The fair way to put it is that rail as a mode is safe, but that doesn’t mean every rail system is well run. Those are two different questions, and the coverage tends to blur them in both directions: “trains are deathtraps” on one side, “nothing to see here” on the other.
Normally, I’d expect further details coming from Madrid in a month or so. But given the upcoming snap election the government faces in less than a month, and the fear that this crash is going to cost the Sánchez government some serious creds he can't afford, I’m thinking we’ll see some added details in somewhat less time... at least before voters go to the polls.
I'll be watching.

Photo: Reuters
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.
One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages.
David Gomez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El Pais.
“People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought,” until emergency services arrived, he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, said the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Passenger Ignacio Relano was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

- By Reuters -
- Oct 28, 2026
URDA, SPAIN: At least 68 people died when two Spanish high-speed trains collided on Wednesday, with rescuers scouring the wreckage for more bodies after Spain’s second deadly rail accident this year and Europe’s deadliest since 2013.
Spain’s transport minister said Wednesday’s crash south of Madrid occurred after a Renfe train was authorised to continue its journey despite there being an active red signal because of a stationary train on the track ahead.
Oscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped traffic, and an erroneous decision had been made to restart the Renfe train, in a breach of protocol.
Ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters were parked next to one of the trains on an elevated section of track, while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage were strewn across an embankment down which at least three carriages had plunged.
RESCUERS LOOKING FOR MORE VICTIMS
Evacuated passengers streamed along a nearby road. Some were splattered with blood or had bandaged wounds, while others wheeled suitcases and were handed water by volunteers.
Miguel, who was travelling with several colleagues in the rear carriage of one of the trains, described the moment of the accident and its immediate aftermath.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,” he told COPE radio.
The head of Castilla-La Mancha’s regional government said the death toll had risen to 68, while rescue workers were still going carriage by carriage looking for other crash victims.
OPERATOR RENFE SAYS CIRCUMSTANCES BEING INVESTIGATED
The collision comes after an accident in January between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators and on the same line that killed 46 people.
In that crash a train derailed and smashed into an oncoming train near Adamuz, in Cordoba province, prompting a debate about the level of investment in railway maintenance in recent years.
A person briefed on Wednesday’s disaster said a train operated by private consortium Iryo stopped near Toledo on orders from infrastructure manager Adif due to a signal fault.
A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said.
Renfe said in a statement that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know”.
“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.
There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Adif.
PASSENGER DESCRIBES SEEING FATALITIES
Authorities gave no immediate figure for the number of injured but Health Minister Mónica García urged people in a post on X to donate blood. Castilla-La Mancha region spokesperson Esther Padilla said 147 people had been travelling on the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe train.
The accident is the deadliest in Europe since a 2013 crash in Spain’s Santiago de Compostela left 80 people dead.
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Cadena SER radio she felt a strong impact that threw her forward, initially making her think the train had made an emergency stop.
She only realised the seriousness of the accident after seeing injured people and being told to evacuate.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she saw what she described as a catastrophic scene, with part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage.
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said. “I saw dead people,” she said.
The Renfe and Iryo trains crashed just after 9 a.m., causing two Iryo wagons to derail, a spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha region said.
Renfe said it had activated a special line for families of victims and expressed its condolences. Iryo said it had activated emergency protocols.
The causes of the January accident near Cordoba are still under investigation. A preliminary report by Spain’s Civil Guard in February pointed to defects in the track, rail or weld between two sections of track as the main hypothesis for the accident, but kept seven other theories open.
ELECTION DUE NEXT MONTH
The latest accident comes as Spain gears up for an election on November 29. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was on his way to the scene of the crash, his office said. The opposition People’s Party cancelled all campaign events, a spokesperson said.
“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo. My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families,” Sanchez said on X.
Accidents, including derailments and collisions, increased from 45 in 2016 to 57 in 2024 and 69 last year, according to Spain’s railway safety authority.
Some 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain in the first half of the year, a decline of roughly 14% compared with the same period last year, according to a Reuters analysis of data from Spain’s competition authority.
European Commission data shows Spain’s maintenance investment in its roughly 4,000 km (2,485 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged large European peers, despite an unmatched drive to expand the network.
Spain spent an average of about €1.5 billion a year from 2018 to 2022 on its high-speed network, more than any other country. The vast majority went to new infrastructure with only some 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.

The collision involved two trains travelling on the Madrid-to-Seville route, with the impact causing carriages to derail and leaving a large-scale emergency response under way.
The BBC’s live coverage of the crash initially reported 10 deaths as authorities warned that the number of victims could rise. Subsequent reports placed the death toll at 64 as further information emerged from the scene.

The impact derailed carriages, with two reported to have fallen down an embankment.
Emergency personnel were dispatched to the area to assist passengers, search the wreckage and transport injured people for medical treatment.
Reuters reported that the collision had claimed at least 64 lives, citing information from Spanish authorities. The incident is the country’s second major deadly train crash this year, following a January collision that killed 46 people.
Emergency services, including firefighters, medical teams and helicopters, were deployed to the crash site. Authorities have been coordinating rescue operations and assessing the scale of the damage.
The collision also disrupted rail travel, with services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia suspended following the incident.
The route is an important connection between Spain’s capital and the southern region of Andalusia, as the suspension is expected to affect passengers travelling along the corridor while authorities and rail operators respond to the crash.

Spain suffered its second deadly high-speed train accident this year when one train on Wednesday slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, with the impact shredding cars and killing at least 64 people.
The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January.
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.
One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages.
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows … We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought,” until emergency services arrived, he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, said the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car torn into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.
“It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy,” García said.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said civil protection authorities had asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was “dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo.”
“Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers,” wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. “All my thoughts are with the victims and their families.”

“We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo),” the royal couple said. “We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”

Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when a IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
The January incident shook confidence in the European country’s extensive high-speed rail service.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.

“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 124 mph for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
“I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts,” Puente said.

Second fatal train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a 13-foot slope.

Spain’s 4 deadly train crashes this year, at a glance
Wednesday’s collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain was the second fatal crash in nine months on a network long held up as a national success story
PARIS -- Wednesday’s deadly collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain was the second fatal crash in nine months on a network that has long been a source of national pride.
Spain has spent decades building Europe’s largest high-speed rail network, second only to China’s.
Until this year, there had been no fatal incidents on its dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992, officials said.
That ended with the disaster near Adamuz, which killed 46 people in January.
That crash and Wednesday's both involved trains run by the state-owned company RENFE and private company IRYO on the track linking Madrid with the Andalusia region.
The year has also seen fatal incidents on a commuter line near Barcelona and at a railroad crossing in central Spain.
A look at four fatal train incidents in Spain this year:
Two high-speed trains, both traveling from Madrid to Seville, collided near Urda, in Toledo province, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, regional authorities said.
One train struck the rear of another that had stopped, derailing two cars. The crash halted high-speed services between Madrid and Andalusia.
An Iryo train traveling from Malaga to Madrid derailed near Adamuz, in southern Spain, and collided with an oncoming Renfe train heading to Huelva.
Forty-six people were killed and more than 100 injured. The impact sent the Renfe train’s first two cars down an embankment.
Investigators’ preliminary findings indicated that a fracture in the rail appeared to predate the derailment.
A commuter train crashed near Gelida, outside Barcelona, after a retaining wall collapsed onto the tracks during heavy rain.
One person was killed and 41 were injured, according to the Spanish government.
The accident came two days after the Adamuz disaster and was followed by a suspension of Catalonia’s Rodalies commuter services.
A passenger train traveling from Madrid to Badajoz struck a car at a railroad crossing near Talavera de la Reina, in Toledo province.
The car’s driver was killed. None of the 206 passengers aboard the train was injured, according to regional emergency services.
Rail traffic was interrupted and replacement transportation arranged for passengers.

sources.text:
AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another after the second such accident to strike Spain this year.
Some carriages were lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment, while dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site.
“We are speaking of approximately 64 (dead), but this is probably going to grow even more,” Castilla-La Mancha’s leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene, raising a previous toll of 31.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.
Helicopters hovered above the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.
State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
Iryo said in a statement that its train, which was carrying 147 passengers and five staff including the driver, “was hit from behind” by the Renfe service.
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, 49, who lives in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
Ortiz added that the passengers of the Iryo told him their train was stationary when the collision happened, describing a “horrific, horrible” scene that “smelled of an accident, of metal”.
Rail safety under scrutiny
The accident comes one month before Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year’s first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on Nov 29.
Sanchez’s office said he was heading to the scene. The premier had said on X that he was “shocked” by the accident and sent “my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families”.
Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was “shocked and concerned” by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
An EU spokeswoman said the bloc was “ready to help Spain if needed”, while European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” with the victims after the “devastating news”.
The Spanish football federation postponed 24 matches in the first round of the Copa del Rey “as a mark of respect and solidarity”.
Spain’s high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world’s second-largest after China and a source of national pride.
However, Wednesday’s accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country’s railways.
That crash was Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year’s accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville.
The cause of the latest disaster, which happened on a straight stretch of track in sunny, dry conditions, was unknown. Five people wearing white overalls were examining the tracks and taking photographs, AFP saw.
One of the country’s busiest routes, it was Spain’s first high-speed line when it opened in 1992 to coincide with the Seville universal exposition.

Spanish authorities initially reported 10 deaths on Wednesday, but Spanish state-owned news agency EFE later reported 30, and sources from the local government in Castilla-La Mancha reported that the death toll had risen to 64 as of the afternoon. The number is still expected to change.
The crash occurred at around 8:30 a.m. near Urda. It involved a Renfe train and an Iryo train, both traveling from Madrid to Seville, according to Spain’s Transport Ministry. Authorities believe the Renfe train struck the Iryo train from behind, derailing two coaches.
The Renfe train carried 397 passengers, according to the Transport Ministry, while the Iryo train reportedly had 146, including one baby.
About 80 people have also been injured in the accident.
Iryo said in a statement that it had activated all emergency protocols and was working closely with authorities to manage the situation. All of its services departing from Madrid-Puerta de Atocha and traveling along the Southern Corridor have been canceled, and the company has not yet announced when they are expected to resume.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia confirmed that the government was coordinating with other institutions to respond to the crash.
“We are mobilizing all the resources at our disposal and coordinating with all the relevant institutions,” Garcia stated. “I’m working with the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha to provide any resources it may need. My full support and gratitude go to the emergency personnel dispatched to the area.”
The crash will likely bring scrutiny upon the trains’ LZB signaling system — translated to “linear train control” — which is supposed to automatically stop a train if the track is occupied, even if the driver fails to use the brakes. The system uses continuous electronic communication between the track and train to control speeds.
This is the second major public transport accident this year in Spain. The current death toll makes the crash deadlier than January’s Adamuz crash, which killed 46 people, injured 152, and prompted Spanish train drivers to call for a three-day strike. Spain’s high-speed railway network reportedly ranks as the largest in Europe and the second biggest in the world after China. Wednesday’s crash is also the third-worst train disaster in the country since the 1970s.

By JOSEPH WILSON and ALICIA LEÓN, Associated Press
URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
“Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
“It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain’s rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the central province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading south in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the IRYO train and the front of the RENFE train.
Samy Paul, a British tourist, described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued from the RENFE train.
“Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down,” he said. “We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over.”
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
“People were trying to get out through the windows … We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived,” he said. “As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg.”
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Transport minister says crash was due to ‘inexplicable’ decision
Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the “inexplicable” order from a central command center for Spain’s trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a “stop signal” active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
“I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts,” Puente said.
Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
“We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact,” he said. “The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.”
Authorities said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.
Spain’s King Felipe VI also visited the crash site.
“We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected,” Spain’s royals said in a statement.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “My heart goes out to the victims’ families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.”
Spain’s soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
Spain already suffered a devastating train crash this year
The wreckage of Wednesday’s crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
Before this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992.
Spain is a leader in high-speed rail
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country’s railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. The Italian-owned IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”
Wilson reported from Barcelona, Spain. Teresa Medrano in Madrid and Iain Sullivan in Urda contributed.

sources.news_title: Spanish high-speed train collision kills at least 64
sources.text:
A high-speed train has slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people in central Spain, authorities say.
Rescue workers were scouring wreckage for more bodies at the crash scene on Wednesday in the province of Toledo.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said "all of Spain" was in mourning after the crash, which Transport Minister Oscar Puente said happened after a Renfe service was authorised to proceed despite an active red signal due to a stationary train ahead.
Puente told reporters in Madrid that the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure, which automatically stopped traffic, but an erroneous decision was then taken to restart the Renfe train.
At the scene in rural Castilla-La Mancha, ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters assembled beside one of the trains on an elevated stretch of track while twisted metal and wreckage lay scattered down an embankment where at least three carriages had plunged.
The head of the regional government Emiliano García-Page said the death toll had risen to 68 while rescuers searching for other victims as darkness fell did not know if other fatalities would be discovered once the carriages were moved.
Passengers removed from the train streamed along a road near the scene, some splattered with blood or with their wounds bandaged, others wheeling suitcases and being given water by volunteers who said it had been donated from neighbouring towns.
Miguel, a passenger travelling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described to COPE radio the moment of the accident.
"We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train," he said.
The disaster, the deadliest train accident in Europe since a 2013 derailment in Spain's Santiago de Compostela in which 80 people died, follows another fatal accident in January involving high-speed trains operated by the same companies on the same line, in which 46 people died.
Renfe said on Wednesday that after being authorised to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary "for reasons we don't know".
"The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation," Renfe said in a statement.
Iryo, which said it had activated emergency protocols, and state-owned infrastructure operator Adif did not respond to requests for comment.
A Castilla-La Mancha government spokesperson said 147 people, including a baby, were on board the Iryo train and 397 on the Renfe service when the crash occurred about 9am, derailing two Iryo carriages.
Passenger Rafael Barcelo said he felt lucky as he had stepped away from his seat for a coffee, adding there had been at least eight victims from his carriage.
"We were having breakfast, drinking a coffee when we felt a very strong impact and we were sent flying," he said.
Renfe said it had opened a special line for families of victims.
The railway operator said it had suspended ticket sales on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed corridor until December 13.
Spanish Health Minister Monica García said emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yebenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
The accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain, according to Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region.

sources.news_title: Spain Train Crash Death Toll Hits 64 in High-Speed Disaster
sources.text:
Spain High-Speed Train Crash Kills 68, Injures Over 100
Transport Minister Oscar Puente told reporters that the collision came after a train restarted its journey despite a halt to all services on a 69-kilometre stretch of track due to a technical failure in an automatic control system
URDA, Spain: A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 68 people and injured scores more on Wednesday, authorities said, in one of Europe's deadliest such disasters this century.
	   The second such accident to strike Spain this year will raise fresh questions about the country's rail safety, with the transport minister speaking of an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the crash.
	   AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side at the bottom of an embankment strewn with debris.
	   The constant to-and-fro of emergency services vehicles continued at night, with rescuers using a drone, lights and cranes to hoist mangled metal and search for further victims in the cold.
	   Castilla-La Mancha's leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene that 68 people had died, raising an earlier toll of 64.
	   "We don't know if another body might appear when the carriages are moved," he added.
	   A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured, with 15 in a critical condition.
	   Pablo Mejia, 42, told AFP that he had miraculously survived with injuries to his head after changing his seat.
	   With blood staining his grey jumper, he recounted "a very strong hit. It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos."
 'Horrible' scene 
	   A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, who lives in the village of Urda close to the site of the accident, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
	   Ortiz, 49, described a "horrific, horrible" scene that "smelled of an accident, of metal".
	   State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
	   Transport Minister Oscar Puente told reporters that the collision came after a train restarted its journey despite a halt to all services on a 69-kilometre stretch of track due to a technical failure in an automatic control system.
	   "The decision to resume traffic, while that system had not been restored, belongs to the control centre," which restarted traffic "in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable", Puente said.
	   The Renfe train restarted and travelled 25 kilometres until it collided with the stationary Iryo, at a speed that could have reached "up to 200 kilometres per hour", Puente added.
	   The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", Puente said.
	   - Rail safety under scrutiny -
	   The accident comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year's first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.
	   He said Spain would observe three days of mourning from Thursday, conceding it was "not acceptable" that two high-speed collisions could happen within months. His Socialists halted campaign activities.
	   The leader of the main opposition conservative Popular Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who leads in most polls, also suspended campaigning but said: "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure."
	   Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was "shocked and concerned", conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
	   Spain's high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the second-largest in the world after China's and a source of national pride.
	   Almost 26 million passengers used the network between January and August this year, according to official statistics.
	   But Wednesday's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country's railways.
	   That crash was Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
( Source : AFP )
