sources.news_title: Spain train crash leaves at least 64 dead in second major collision this year
sources.text:
BARCELONA, Spain — At least 68 people were killed and 68 injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, sending carriages careering off the tracks, in the second major accident on the same line in less than a year.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail,” one passenger, Miguel, told Spain’s COPE radio, adding that he was traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains.
“Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train — I imagine it must have been the other one,” he added.
Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo.
As rescue teams continued to search through the wreckage of the derailed carriages, the Castilla-La Mancha regional government said 68 people had been killed and 68 injured. Together the two trains were carrying more than 500 passengers.
Several U.S. citizens were among the injured, according to a State Department spokesperson, who said the U.S. is continuing to work with local authorities to identify all Americans involved and provide them consular assistance.
“We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of all those affected,” the spokesperson said. “We encourage U.S. citizens in the area to notify loved ones of their safety and monitor local media for updates.”
At the site of the crash on Wednesday, Prime Minister of Spain Pedro Sánchez said: “The government of Spain and the whole state are with the victims and also with the families of the victims.”
Sánchez, who is facing a snap election next month, said the government was investigating the cause of the crash and any failures, vowing action “if there has been negligence.”
He said that the country must restore confidence in its high-speed rail network, with the crash coming after a separate disaster on the same rail line killed 46 people in January. “It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to have two high-speed accidents in less than a year,” he said.
Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, said the crash occurred around 8:53 a.m. Wednesday following a combination of technical and human errors.
Puente said that at around 8:30 a.m., a computer failure led the control system near the station in Urda, Spain, to crash, with a red signal issued, causing several trains in the area to be automatically stopped in place. With the computer system down, rail traffic was then handed over to a control center.
The control center communicated with the stopped trains, Puente said, and the decision was made at approximately 8:36 a.m. to authorize a state-owned Renfe high-speed train to resume its normal journey, despite the fact that there was a stationary train from private rail company Iryo on the tracks ahead.
An erroneous decision was made to restart the Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.
Locals rushed to the scene of the accident, which has prompted a major national emergency response and raised questions about the safety and security of Spain’s high-speed rail infrastructure, which had previously been hailed as among the most sophisticated in Europe.
“We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived,” David Gómez, a construction worker who was working nearby and ran to help, told the newspaper El País.
“As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg,” he said.
Spain’s royal family said it shared “in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Spanish political parties said Wednesday they would briefly pause campaigning ahead of next month’s general election. Spain’s football federation also said it would postpone some of its Copa del Rey soccer fixtures following the collision.
Aerial video shows aftermath of deadly crash
Juan Manuel Moreno, the president of the Andalusian regional government, said on X that there would be three days of mourning in the region.
Eduarda, a passenger on the Iryo train, told Spain’s Cadena SER radio that she felt a strong impact that threw her forward and she initially thought the train had made an emergency stop.
After climbing down an embankment to safety, she said she saw part of the train hanging down the slope and a fire in one carriage. “I saw dead people,” she added.
Salvador Arriza, a 62-year-old employee of Airbus, was traveling near the rear of the Renfe train.
He told the Reuters news agency the carriage ended up “completely wrecked, with seats being ripped out.”
“I was lucky because I was in a backward-facing seat, and the impact pushed me into it,” he added. “After the first hit I was disoriented, but the worst thing was that the train then kept moving for quite some time from the inertia and that’s when I thought something would happen to me.”
Emergency responders, including a helicopter, police and ambulances, arrived within about 20 minutes, she said.
Police were still inside the trains late on Wednesday searching for additional victims. The crash site was cordoned off, with most of the injured having been taken to a hospital in the city of Toledo, about 30 minutes away.
Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union.
The Spanish Union of Railway Drivers said it would proceed with a planned strike action Thursday “in defense of railway safety.”

The collision occurred near the towns of Mora, Orgaz and Urda.
LONDON -- At least 69 people were killed after two trains collided on Spain's Madrid-Seville high-speed line on Wednesday, officials said.
The collision occurred at around 8:30 a.m. local time at kilometer marker 118 near Urda. The crash involved a Renfe train and an Iryo train, both traveling from Madrid to Seville, Spain's Transport Ministry told ABC News.
The collision was also the second major train crash in Spain this year on the same high-speed train line, involving the same trains from the same rail operators. In January, two high-speed Iryo and Renfe trains collided near Adamuz in the province of Cordoba, killing 46 people. Authorities said one of the trains derailed and another train collided with the derailed cars.
The Spanish Interior Ministry said in a statement Thursday that six more victims were added to the death toll overnight, bringing the total number of people who perished in the crash to 74. The office of the president and the Transportation Ministry later revised that number downward to 69 dead.
During a news conference Wednesday, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente called the crash "truly unbelievable." He said the preliminary investigation indicates the crash was caused by an "inexplicable" order by the rail controllers to allow one train to proceed despite a safety failure that halted a train on the tracks further ahead.
According to Puente, a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control center takes over," Puente said, adding it was the control center which decided to allow the trains to move again without any speed restrictions. That decision, Puente said, resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
In addition to those killed, at least 15 people were seriously injured and were taken to area hospitals, and more than 50 were hospitalized with lesser injuries, Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the Castilla-La Mancha Region, said during a separate news conference on Wednesday.
Garcia-Page said 24 victims who were killed were found on the Renfe train and the remainder were on the Iryo train. He said search-and-rescue crews are using canines to comb through the wreckage looking for victims.
"All of Spain is mourning. We express our solidarity and deepest sympathy to the relatives of the victims," Garcia-Page said.
Garcia-Page continued, "The ministry is trying to determine the causes of this terrible tragedy and understand how and why it happened. We are going to get to the bottom of this. And if there was any negligence, it will come to light. If there were failures in the safety system, we will address them decisively."
The incident marked the deadliest high-speed train crash in Spain since 2013, when 80 people were killed and more than 170 were injured when a train traveling from Madrid to Ferrol derailed in Galicia in northwest Spain.
"We have suffered two terrible high-speed rail tragedies in a single year. Everything appears to indicate that the causes of both accidents are unrelated, but it is not for me to say," Garcia-Page said at Wednesday's news conference. "That is the role of the independent railway accident investigation commission."
He added, "If we need to further strengthen safety in order to restore confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because it is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have."
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who traveled on Wednesday to the site of the crash, said in a social media statement that he is "shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo."
"We extend all our solidarity to the families of the victims and to the injured, to whom we wish a speedy recovery. Our main priority is the victims," Sánchez said.
The government of Spain announced on Wednesday that it has declared three days of official morning, from Thursday to Saturday, to honor those killed and injured in the crash.
"We'd like to convey to the families our condolences, our sorrow, our support and our affection at such a hard, difficult time," Spain's King Felipe VI said in a statement.
As part of the preliminary investigation of Wednesday's crash, authorities said the Renfe train probably struck the Iryo train from behind, causing two coaches to derail and plummet down an embankment.
The Iryo train was carrying 146 passengers, including one baby, while the Renfe train had 397 passengers, according to the transport ministry.
"It was a terrible crash. The carriage partially overturned. We saw carriages next to it completely wrecked," crash survivor Miguel Ángel Pérez told RTVE, the Spanish national radio and television public broadcasting network.
Ángel Pérez said he was riding with work colleagues in the last car of the Renfe train when the crash occurred. He said that prior to the crash train operators warned that the train was stopping due to "an overload on the track."
"Then it started moving again, and that's when we felt immense impact. We felt the train move, derail and we were tilted. It was a terrible few seconds," Ángel Pérez said.
An American tourist named Dire and his wife said they were headed to Andalusia and were also on the train that had stopped on the tracks before they felt "a huge crash."
"The train moved, things flew everywhere," Dire of Florida told the Spanish news station, Canal 24 Horas. "I looked out the window and saw that the train was completely destroyed. People were screaming, crying, covered in blood... I told my wife, 'We have to leave now,' because we were afraid the train would overturn."
Another passenger, Ana, told reporters that she was traveling on one of the trains with her sister and her dog when the crash occurred, according to Reuters.
"Suddenly, I only heard screams," Ana, who suffered injuries to her face and leg, told Reuters.
In the aftermath of the crash, Ana said passengers broke windows and that firefighters pulled her from the wreckage. "I was covered in blood," she said.
She described the horrific scene of seeing people dying in front of her.
"Some people were fine, and others were really bad. You could see them dying, and you could do nothing," said Ana, who added that she and her sister, who was also injured, were taken to a hospital by ambulance.
In a statement, Iryo said its service 6076, traveling from Madrid to Seville, was involved in the accident near Urda. The company said it had activated all emergency protocols and was working closely with authorities to manage the situation.
As a result of the crash, all Iryo services departing from Madrid-Puerta de Atocha and traveling along the Southern Corridor have been canceled. The company said it had no estimate for when service would resume.
Spain's Health Minister Monica Garcia said the government was mobilizing resources and coordinating with relevant institutions to respond to the crash.
“We are mobilizing all the resources at our disposal and coordinating with all the relevant institutions,” Garcia said. “I’m working with the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha to provide any resources it may need. My full support and gratitude go to the emergency personnel dispatched to the area."
The U.S. State Department confirms that several U.S. citizens were injured.
"The Department of State and the U.S. Embassy in Madrid are working closely with local authorities to assist Americans,” a department spokesperson said. "We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of all those affected.”
The department is asking Americans in need of assistance and those concerned about the safety of loved ones in Spain to get in contact. So far, it has not indicated that any U.S. citizens are among the dead.

At least 64 people are confirmed dead — and the count is still rising — after a Renfe AVE train plowed into the rear of a stationary Iryo service near Urda, in Toledo province, on Wednesday morning, knocking two Iryo wagons off the rails and triggering the largest rail emergency response Spain has seen in over a decade. The 64-death figure was confirmed to CNN by the Castilla-La Mancha regional government; earlier counts fluctuated between 10 and 46 as crews worked through badly damaged carriages.
The disaster lands nine months after the January 18 Adamuz collision in Córdoba province, in which an Iryo train derailed at night and slid onto an adjacent track, where it was struck by an oncoming Renfe service — a crash that ultimately killed 46 people, including the Renfe train's driver, making it Spain's deadliest rail disaster in over a decade at that point. Both disasters involve the same pair of operators: state-owned Renfe and private competitor Iryo.
A Stopped Train, a Green Signal, and Catastrophic Consequences
The collision unfolded at approximately 8:54 a.m. local time on a flat, straight section of track between the towns of Los Yébenes and Urda, more than 100 kilometers south of Madrid. The Iryo train had halted on the line for reasons that remain under investigation — and the Renfe AVE traveling directly behind it was apparently cleared to advance on the same track. Initial accounts point to operational or human error as the most likely cause, though no official determination has been issued.
The impact was catastrophic. Passenger Patricia Álvarez, aboard the Renfe train, told CNN that riders were "hurled into the air" at the moment of collision. Aerial footage showed two Iryo wagons splayed sideways off the track — one of them torn open — with fragments of metal and carriage material scattered across the surrounding farmland. Military units, police forces, firefighters, and civil protection teams converged on the crash site from across the region.
Urda's mayor, Manuel Galán, coordinated with regional civil protection authorities to open a local sports pavilion as an emergency triage area, accommodating victims beyond the capacity of field medical teams.
How the Death Toll Climbed Through the Morning
Regional emergency services initially recorded 10 deaths. Castilla-La Mancha spokeswoman Esther Padilla warned reporters in the first hour that the toll would "surely rise." By midday, regional president Emiliano García-Page confirmed 32 dead; a regional government spokesperson subsequently confirmed 64 deaths to CNN as rescue teams cleared additional sections of wreckage. The Castilla-La Mancha government also told Agence France-Presse that the final count remained open as work continued.
Spain's Health Ministry described the events near Toledo as a "major tragedy." Injured passengers were transferred to regional hospitals throughout the morning; no confirmed total on the number of hospitalized victims had been announced as of the time of publication.
The Same Two Operators — A Different Type of Crash, the Same Corridor
Wednesday's disaster is the second catastrophic accident on the Madrid–Andalusia high-speed corridor to involve both Renfe and Iryo within the same calendar year — though the mechanics differ. The January Adamuz crash began when an Iryo train derailed and crossed onto an adjacent track, where a Renfe train approaching from the opposite direction struck it; that collision involved two trains on parallel lines. The October 28 crash was a rear-end collision: one train was motionless on the track, and the trailing train drove into it. Adamuz's death toll reached 46 by January 31 — now surpassed by Toledo's preliminary count of 64.
Iryo entered Spain's high-speed rail market in 2022 as the country's first private competitor to Renfe on the high-speed network. Iryo confirmed it had activated all emergency protocols after the collision. Renfe, for its part, posted a statement on X extending condolences to victims and their families. Spain's royal family released a statement saying the Crown was "moved and concerned" by the unfolding situation in Toledo.
Strike, Suspension, and a Rail System Under Scrutiny
The crash compounds what was already a difficult week for Spanish rail. A 24-hour nationwide strike by Renfe train drivers, called by union SEMAF on October 16 over stalled negotiations on safety protocols, personnel conditions, and rolling-stock reliability, was already set for Thursday, October 29 — the day after the collision. Authorities confirmed the labor action and the crash are independent events, even as the strike's safety-related demands are now harder to dismiss.
Rail infrastructure manager ADIF confirmed the suspension of all high-speed services between Madrid, Ciudad Real, and Andalusia in both directions following the collision. Renfe announced that passengers holding tickets on AVE, Avlo, and connecting Iryo routes would receive free changes or full refunds.
The investigation is active. Early accounts point toward a signaling or operational failure that allowed the Renfe train to advance onto track already occupied by the stopped Iryo service — but no official ruling has been handed down. Spain operates Europe's largest high-speed rail network, with nearly 4,000 kilometers of dedicated track built for speeds above 250 km/h. That distinction, once a marker of modern ambition and engineering pride, now carries a weight that no infrastructure milestone can lighten.

High-speed train collision kills dozens in Spain
A high-speed train has crashed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 30 people in central Spain.
Spanish authorities initially reported 10 deaths, but state-owned news agency EFE and other media reported later that the death toll had risen to at least 30.
It was the second major train accident in Spain in 2026.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred on Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo.
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain.
One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
She said the cause of the crash was not known.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Y?benes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia told TVE that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars.
She said the injured were being sent to hospitals in the area.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO.
It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported.
Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said it had "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities".
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galan, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.
A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez cancelled his agenda to focus on the crash, writing on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo".
"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sanchez, who faces a national election in November.
Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.
"We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected," the royal couple said.
The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano Garc?a-Page, wrote on X that he was on his way to the crash site.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train.
The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.

Spain train crash kills at least 68 as Prime minister says ‘Whole country is grieving’
At least 68 people have been killed and scores injured after two high-speed trains collided in Spain, triggering a major emergency response and leaving the country mourning the victims.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed condolences to the victims and their families, acknowledging the scale of the tragedy and its impact on the nation.
“The whole country is grieving,” Sánchez said, expressing solidarity with those affected by the disaster.
Emergency services, including firefighters, police officers, medical personnel and rescue workers, were deployed to the scene to search for survivors, recover victims and assist injured passengers.
Authorities have launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collision, with initial accounts pointing to a computer failure and subsequent decisions by railway control officials.

COMPUTER FAILURE PRECEDED COLLISION
Spain’s Transport Minister, Óscar Puente, provided further details about the circumstances leading to the collision, describing the accident as “truly unbelievable”.
According to Puente, a computer failure initially brought six moving trains to a halt, including the Renfe and Iryo trains that were subsequently involved in the crash.
He explained that when a system failure occurs, responsibility for managing train movements shifts to the railway control centre.
“In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over,” Puente said, adding that the control centre subsequently authorised the trains to resume their journeys without imposing speed restrictions.
The minister described the decision to allow the trains to move again as having been made “under inexplicable circumstances”.
The decision resulted in the Renfe train colliding with the Iryo train, which was stationary further along the tracks.
Investigators are expected to examine the computer failure, the decisions taken by the control centre and the circumstances in which the trains were authorised to resume their journeys.
GOVERNMENT EXPRESSES CONDOLENCES
Sánchez said emergency services were working to assist those affected, with authorities coordinating rescue operations and support for passengers and their families.
Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia also expressed sadness over the collision, extending their support to the victims, their relatives and emergency personnel involved in the response.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed solidarity with Spain following the disaster.
INVESTIGATION UNDERWAY
The collision has raised questions about railway safety, signalling systems and operational procedures in Spain, which operates one of Europe’s largest high-speed rail networks.
Investigators are working to establish the sequence of events leading to the crash and determine whether technical failures or operational decisions contributed to the disaster.
Authorities are also working to identify victims, notify relatives and provide medical care to the injured.
As Spain mourns the victims, attention is turning to the investigation and the measures needed to prevent a similar tragedy.
